title: Pons Asinorum in Hyperbolic and Spherical Geometry
description: The parent (isosceles-triangle) proves Euclid I.5 (Pons Asinorum: equal sides ⟹ equal base angles) using Mathlib's inner-product-space geometry. This entry answers its OQ-02: prove the isosceles triangle theorem in hyperbolic and spherical geometry, where no inner product space is available. Working purely from the non-Euclidean laws of cosines (solving for cos A as a symmetric function of the adjacent sides) and the injectivity of cos on [0,π], we prove equal legs imply equal base angles in both geometries, plus the equilateral ⟹ equiangular corollaries. All 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext:
The isosceles triangle theorem — Euclid's Proposition I.5, nicknamed the Pons Asinorum ('bridge of asses') — states that the base angles of a triangle with two equal sides are equal. In Euclidean geometry it follows from triangle congruence or, in a coordinate model, from the inner product structure (the parent gallery entry uses Mathlib's inner-product-space triangle API). In the non-Euclidean geometries of constant curvature — the sphere and the hyperbolic plane — there is no ambient inner product space of the same kind, and the relationship between sides and angles is governed instead by the laws of cosines:

  spherical:  cos a = cos b·cos c + sin b·sin c·cos A,
  hyperbolic: cosh a = cosh b·cosh c − sinh b·sinh c·cos A,

where A is the angle opposite side a and b, c are the two adjacent sides. Solving each for cos A yields an expression that is symmetric in the adjacent sides; the isosceles hypothesis a = b makes the two base-angle cosines identical, and the injectivity of cos on [0, π] (where triangle angles live) upgrades equal cosines to equal angles. This entry formalizes exactly that argument, answering the parent's OQ-02 with no inner product space.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the isosceles triangle theorem (equal sides ⟹ equal base angles) in spherical and hyperbolic geometry without using an inner product space: model a triangle by its sides a, b, c and angles satisfying the appropriate law of cosines, and show a = b ⟹ A = B (with A, B ∈ [0, π]). Derive the equilateral ⟹ equiangular corollaries.
overview.proofStrategy: Solve each law of cosines for the cosine of the angle opposite side a: sphCosA a b c = (cos a − cos b·cos c)/(sin b·sin c) and hypCosA a b c = (cosh b·cosh c − cosh a)/(sinh b·sinh c). The base angle B opposite side b is governed by the same formula with a and b swapped. When a = b, substituting collapses the two expressions to the same value (sph_isosceles_cos / hyp_isosceles_cos, proved by subst + rfl), so cos A = cos B. Since triangle angles lie in [0, π] and cos is injective there (Real.injOn_cos), A = B. The equilateral corollaries apply the equal-cosines step twice.
keyInsights: The non-Euclidean Pons Asinorum needs no inner product space — only the law of cosines, which encodes the side–angle relationship of the geometry, and the injectivity of cos on [0, π].
Solving the law of cosines for cos A produces an expression symmetric in the two adjacent sides; the isosceles hypothesis a = b makes the base-angle cosines literally identical (subst + rfl).
The spherical and hyperbolic cases are the same algebra with cos/sin replaced by cosh/sinh — one structural argument, two geometries.
Triangle angles live in [0, π], exactly the interval on which cos is injective, so equal cosines reliably give equal angles — the only analytic input.
Modelling triangles by their side/angle data plus the law of cosines (rather than by points in a metric space) is what frees the proof from the inner product structure the parent relied on.

sections.mathContext: spherical: $\cos a = \cos b\cos c + \sin b\sin c\cos A$; hyperbolic: $\cosh a = \cosh b\cosh c - \sinh b\sinh c\cos A$.

sections.title: Section I: cos of an Angle from the Law of Cosines
sections.summary: sphCosA and hypCosA solve the spherical and hyperbolic laws of cosines for cos of the angle opposite side a — an expression symmetric in the two adjacent sides b, c.
sections.mathContext: $\mathrm{sphCosA}(a,b,c) = \dfrac{\cos a - \cos b\cos c}{\sin b\sin c}$, $\mathrm{hypCosA}(a,b,c) = \dfrac{\cosh b\cosh c - \cosh a}{\sinh b\sinh c}$.

sections.title: Section II: Algebraic Core — Equal Legs Force Equal Cosines
sections.summary: sph_isosceles_cos / hyp_isosceles_cos: since sphCosA and hypCosA are symmetric in the adjacent sides, a = b makes the two base-angle cosines definitionally equal — proved by subst + rfl alone, no analysis needed.

sections.title: Section III: Pons Asinorum in Both Geometries
sections.summary: spherical_isosceles and hyperbolic_isosceles: equal legs a = b imply equal base angles A = B, via the equal-cosines step and Real.injOn_cos on [0, π]. No inner product space.

sections.mathContext: The natural corollary: a regular (equilateral) non-Euclidean triangle is equiangular.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) proof, in 89 lines with 6 theorems and 2 definitions, of the isosceles triangle theorem (Pons Asinorum) in spherical and hyperbolic geometry, with no inner product space. Solving the non-Euclidean laws of cosines for the base-angle cosine makes it symmetric in the adjacent sides, so equal legs give equal cosines, and injectivity of cos on [0, π] gives equal angles; equilateral ⟹ equiangular follows.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's OQ-02: the isosceles triangle theorem holds in spherical and hyperbolic geometry, proved from the law of cosines alone rather than the inner-product-space machinery the Euclidean case used. The side/angle-with-law-of-cosines modelling is a reusable, coordinate-free way to formalize constant-curvature triangle geometry, and the sphCosA/hypCosA definitions and the equal-cosines lemmas are building blocks for further non-Euclidean triangle results (e.g. the converse, or the law-of-sines).
openQuestions: Prove the converse (equal base angles ⟹ equal opposite sides) in spherical and hyperbolic geometry, using the dual law of cosines that expresses sides in terms of angles.
Derive the spherical and hyperbolic laws of sines in the same coordinate-free framework and combine them with these results toward a full non-Euclidean triangle-congruence toolkit.
